I've been working this land since I was in my twenties. My husband and son mostly work in town now, so I manage the fields myself with help during harvest. 4.1 mu is not much, but I know every inch of it.

The wheat-maize rotation is my backbone — 2.5 mu. I plant wheat in October after the maize comes off, harvest it in June, then turn around and plant maize immediately on the same ground. I've done this my whole life. The cotton I keep on the remaining 1.6 mu, separate. It's hard work to pick at my age, but the income helps when grain prices are low.

I switched to improved and hybrid seeds years ago. The old varieties don't keep up. For cotton I use the Bt types so I don't have to spray nearly as much for bollworm — that alone saves me a lot of effort. For wheat I get improved certified seed from the county station. For maize, hybrid.

On fertilizer, I know my ground. I split the wheat nitrogen — some goes in at planting, the rest I topdress at jointing. I don't pour it all in at once the way some younger farmers do. Maize gets a bit more nitrogen because the hybrid varieties need it. Cotton I balance more evenly because it's pickier.

With my well I can irrigate when I need to. Wheat needs three waterings — at sowing if it's dry, at jointing, and at heading. Maize usually gets two — the summer rains cover most of it. Cotton I water three times, watching the weather.

Pesticides: wheat twice (aphids and rust), maize twice (stem borer, armyworm), cotton three times even with Bt (aphids, spider mites still come).

For tillage I rotary till before wheat every year. Maize I go in no-till right after wheat harvest — no time and it saves moisture. Cotton field I rotary till in spring before transplanting.
